item.title: [andros.dev] Tildes: the shared Unix computers
item.description:
Imagine a computer running somewhere. You connect over SSH with your key. A Unix environment appears in front of you, and pwd shows that you are in your own home directory. You type who and see other people logged into the same machine as you. You don't know who they are, but you can finger them and read their .plan. You can even run write to send them a message that will pop up in their terminal. Someone replies that there is an IRC server where everyone hangs out. You run weechat and join the conversation. They say hello. One user tells you there is more documentation on the "forum", a bulletin board, and that you can open it with bbj. You find plenty of information. Reading the threads, you discover that you have a personal website in ~/public_html, published at https://server/~user/. You quickly run nano ~/public_html/index.html and write a few lines of HTML. You check how it looks with lynx. You send an internal email with alpine to the IRC contact who helped you earlier, thanking them and inviting them to visit your new site. While you wait for an answer, you open tin, the news reader (NNTP), to catch up on the news of your small community.

This is not nostalgia for the 90s: it exists today, and it is called a tilde.

What is a tilde

A tilde is a shared, public access Unix computer. Its admin gives you an account, you log in over SSH and you get your own home directory, your shell, your website, your email and your programs. Resources are shared with the rest of the users: the CPU, the disk, the installed programs, and so on.

It is not a platform, a service or a protocol. It is a machine with Unix, an admin and a community.

Paul Ford, the creator of tilde.club, put it like this:

Tilde.club is one cheap, unmodified Unix computer on the Internet.

In practice, almost all of them share these features:

  • A shell account: you log in with ssh user@server and work in the terminal as if it were your own computer.
  • A personal website: whatever you save in ~/public_html is published at https://server/~user/.
  • A local community: IRC chat, internal email, terminal forums and classic commands to see who is online.

They are non-profit: they run on donations and on the time of one or more volunteer admins. And this works because they are small servers, from a dozen to a few thousand users.

Why it is called a tilde

Because of the ~ symbol. On Unix, the tilde stands for your home directory. As Paul Ford said, it is a little like the @ on Twitter, a shortcut that says "here is a person".

Here is an anecdote you can tell your grandchildren. That use of the tilde comes from the Lear-Siegler ADM-3A terminal from the 1970s, where the ~ key and the Home key were the same.

The Tildeverse

The Tildeverse describes itself as "a loose association of like-minded tilde communities". There is no central authority. Each server has its own admins and rules, but they share services and interests. One tilde may only offer Gemini and Gopher, while another has IRC, Mastodon and live radio. The key is that users can move between them and meet: it is a federation of servers, not of applications.

As I write these lines, it has 13 members: aussies.space, cosmic.voyage, ctrl-c.club, envs.net, rw.rs, texto-plano.xyz, tilde.club, tilde.green, tilde.guru, tilde.institute, tilde.pink, tilde.team and tilde.town. If you like to poke around, the full list is available as JSON, with the creation date, operating system and admins of each one. There is a bit of everything: Debian, Fedora, OpenBSD, FreeBSD and even NetBSD.

On top of the servers there is a layer of shared services:

  • tilde.chat: the Tildeverse IRC network (irc.tilde.chat, port 6697 with TLS), with web chat, an XMPP gateway and a Mumble server.
  • tilde.zone: a Mastodon instance for tilde users.
  • tilde.news: a link aggregator in the style of Hacker News.
  • tilderadio.org: a radio station with live DJs. "It's radio minus radio."
  • tildegit.org: a Git forge for community projects.
  • Also: a terminal forum (bbj), a zine, a shared journal, a pastebin and Gopher space.

Nobody forces you to use every service, to socialize or to explore the Tildeverse. But the fun is in bumping into people from your server or from others.

House rules

Each tilde has its own code of conduct, and almost all of them fit in one line. This is tilde.club's:

No drama. Be respectful. Have fun.

tilde.town's is even shorter: "Be kind to each other". But behind the brevity there are clear rules:

  • No cryptocurrency mining: on tilde.town it means an immediate and permanent ban.
  • Nothing commercial: your web space is not for business or advertising.
  • Don't hog resources: the machine belongs to everyone. Don't use it as a backup drive, a proxy or a backend for your IDE.
  • No port scanning and no VPNs: tilde.team bans them, and it has also added a very 2026 rule: no AI agents or services on the server.

My favorite is the motto of texto-plano.xyz, the Spanish-speaking tilde: "let's be few but united". It sums up the philosophy better than any manifesto. A small community is not a limitation, it is the goal. That is why signup forms ask what interests you about the server: they want to make sure there is a curious human being on the other side.

Tildes to explore

Here is my list of active tildes, with their website, approximate number of users and some notes. It may be different tomorrow, but you can keep in mind that the most popular one is tilde.town, with almost 4,000 users.

# Tilde Approx. users Notes
1 tilde.town ~3,900 Very active, its own IRC
2 tilde.club ~3,000 to 4,400 The original, news in 2026
3 tilde.team ~2,400 Wiki, webmail, IRC
4 envs.net ~1,560 Lots of services
5 sdf.org No public list The oldest (1987), has Mastodon
6 tilde.institute ~950 OpenBSD
7 ctrl-c.club ~825 From 2014, latest news in 2023
8 rw.rs ~217 Signups through GitHub
9 tilde.green ~158 Open signups, wiki
10 texto-plano.xyz ~80 In Spanish: radio, podcast and magazine
11 tilde.guru ~67 FreeBSD
12 tilde.fun ~40 Small
13 aussies.space 11 Tiny
14 cosmic.voyage No list Collaborative science fiction
15 republic.circumlunar.space No list Gopher, web and Gemini hosting
16 rawtext.club No list Rebuilding from scratch
17 tilde.pink No list Gopher and Gemini only
18 blinkenshell.org No list Active wiki
19 dimension.sh No list Little visible activity
20 hashbang.sh No list Online

SDF deserves a special mention. It is the grandfather of them all, with almost 40 years behind it, and it works with a different model: the basic account is free, and a one-time fee of $36 (ARPA) gives you lifetime access to more services.

Not everything is pretty

Tildes are machines with people behind them, and that comes with risks.

In May 2026, tilde.town had to close access because of a kernel vulnerability with no patch available. It opened, closed and reopened over two weeks, disabling kernel modules and replacing Nginx with Caddy.

In August it was tilde.team's turn. Someone got root access and ran rm -rf /. Daily backups limited the loss to a few hours, but they had to disable SSH and move the shared Tildeverse services to another machine.

Sharing a computer with thousands of strangers has a price:

  • You depend on the admin. If they get tired, fall ill or lose interest, the server disappears. Grex closed in 2023 after 32 years, and the list of dead tildes is long.
  • Root sees everything. Your files live on someone else's machine. Don't keep secrets there.
  • Security is shared. A kernel bug or a compromised account affects the whole community.
  • Your identity is borrowed. ~user@server is yours as long as the server exists, just like an account on a Mastodon instance.

These are risks you should know and accept before requesting your account.

Final notes

Tildes are a corner that makes the internet a nicer place: you log in, say hello, see who is around, learn new commands, edit your website and read the news. A place shared with people as curious as you.

In 2014, Paul Ford wrote that when people talk about "cloud computing" they are talking about "millions of tiny ghost towns": servers running where nobody lives. A tilde is the exact opposite: a small town that smells of coffee, with neighbors who greet and help each other.

If you end up joining a tilde, I would love to finger you. ;)

Sources

  • Tilde.Club: I had a couple drinks and woke up with 1,000 nerds, Paul Ford's account (October 9, 2014) of how tilde.club was born. His quotes come from here: the cheap Unix computer, the ~ as the @ and the ghost towns of the cloud.
  • tilde.club: its code of conduct, its signup form and its wiki, where the commands in the introduction come from: the command line guide (bbj, lynx, alpine, nano), the IRC page (weechat) and the tin page.
  • Tildeverse, its member list and the JSON version.
  • tilde.chat, tilde.zone, tilde.news, tilderadio.org and tildegit.org, the shared services of the Tildeverse.
  • tilde.town: its code of conduct and its blog, with the May 2026 kernel vulnerability lockdown.
  • tilde.team, with the notice about the August 2026 attack and its terms of service.
  • texto-plano.xyz and its code of conduct.
  • SDF Public Access Unix System on Wikipedia, for its history, and the SDF join page, for current prices.
  • The Grex shutdown notice from 2023 and its history.
  • Tilde on Wikipedia, on the origin of ~ as the home directory and the ADM-3A terminal.
  • I checked the user counts and the status of each tilde by visiting their websites and user lists on October 19, 2026.

item.title: [andros.dev] The Photoshop clone that hurts GIMP
item.description:
We are seeing a wave of "X rebuilt in pure Y" projects: clones of the most expensive proprietary software. In just a few weeks, someone has published a replica of almost the entire Adobe and Microsoft Office catalog, written in Rust by Claude. PhotoCraft, a Photoshop clone. WordCraft, a Word clone. FigCraft, a Figma clone. And more projects are on the way.

From a distance, it may look like a checkmate against companies like Adobe or Microsoft. In reality, it is a move against open source. We are building free alternatives to free software, not to proprietary software. Professionals pay for the license because they want things to work and be compatible; they don't care about alternatives. Whoever installs a clone is someone who never wanted to pay Adobe in the first place. The same person who would have downloaded GIMP or Krita. A user who could have discovered a free project, and maybe even contributed to it one day, ends up with a broken version and no support.

Behind every open source project there are years or decades of accumulated knowledge, of very specific and very specialized contributions. GIMP was born in 1995 as a class project by two Berkeley students, and LibreOffice descends from StarWriter, a word processor from 1985. Every fixed line has a story behind it: a document that broke its layout, a printer that didn't work properly, a .docx with twenty years of inherited styles. A clone can imitate the behavior it observes, but not the accumulated wisdom.

Then there is the lack of friction. Without the effort of learning or contributing, there is no long-term bond, let alone a community. I wrote about this in I closed pull requests and issues on my projects, and I'm happier, in case you want to dig deeper. A project needs frustration, reward and communication to be sustainable. Whoever drops a prompt into your project today will drop it into a more fun one tomorrow.

I'm not against using AI to code: I use it every day. I'm against where the effort is going. All that energy, all that money spent on tokens, could be fixing the interface or the documentation of an existing project, or improving its compatibility. But contributing to something old is boring, and cloning popular software is fun: it gives you the feeling of having beaten Adobe over a weekend. Meanwhile, the one really getting weaker is the free software ecosystem.

Free software isn't defended by cloning it. It's defended by using it and contributing to it. Instead of inviting people to use a clone, buy a virtual coffee for the developer behind your favorite free alternative.

item.title: [andros.dev] We don't want decentralized systems, we want small ones
item.description:
We don't want distributed systems, we want small systems. It doesn't matter if they are centralized inside: what matters is that they stay at a manageable size. That makes them cheap, easy to maintain and almost free of moderation. One example is tildes, shared Unix servers where every user has their own account. They run on a trusted admin and donations. When they grow too big, more tildes appear. Another example is Friend Camp, a community of friends. It costs about $30 a month, around $1 per person.

Despite being centralized, they feel like the opposite of big platforms. There are no commercial interests and people know each other. It's like a shoe shop in a small town. The shop can only serve a few customers because there is little space, you know the owner's name (maybe even his wife's) and the shelves don't offer much variety; and yet you know you will be well served and the owner wants you to leave with what is best for you. In a big department store, on the other hand, the staff don't care whether you come back or not. The owner might be a board of shareholders who only want to maximize profit. Space is unlimited, but there are queues and it's hard to get help. You don't even know if the product is what you are looking for, even if it is cheaper. Welcome to economies of scale. Now apply that to centralized systems.

Distributed systems make us feel in control, because resources are shared among all participants. In return, they only ask us to provide the hardware and the time to maintain it. And that is where they clash with what Moxie Marlinspike said: "People do not want to run their own servers" (2022). Maybe we don't have the time, the money or the knowledge to be a node in a distributed network. Maybe we already have enough with our lives without also having to keep an eye on our mail server. So we end up using a centralized provider inside a distributed system: GitHub or GitLab when we want to use Git, Gmail or Outlook when we want to use email, or WordPress.com or Medium when we want to publish a blog. The small system solves the dilemma without giving up what matters: one person provides the server and the time for everyone else, and the rest only need to trust someone they know. Isn't that too much load for one person? Not if the community is small. Darius Kazemi, with about 50 active users on Friend Camp, gets on average one moderation request a month.

Take three Mastodon instances as an example: icosahedron.website (about 133 monthly active users), mastodon.technology (about 23,600 accounts) and mastodon.social (about 3.4 million accounts). All three run the same software and the same protocol; the only thing that changes is size. The second one shut down in 2022 because its only admin burned out. The other two are still alive, but for different reasons: the first because it is small, and the third because it has plenty of resources (in 2024, the organization that runs it brought in about 2.19 million euros, almost all of it from donations).

The biggest risk for a volunteer-run community is almost always the same: that whoever maintains it burns out. That is why size is not a detail: it is what keeps the work within what one person can handle. Limiting size with waiting lists, closed registrations or a cap on active users seems counterintuitive, but it works. To grow without burning out, there are only two paths left: raise a lot of money, like mastodon.social, or become a business, like Reddit, X or YouTube. But profit guarantees neither better quality nor better service. My small Forgejo instance is as centralized as GitHub, but it has 10 active users: it has gone down fewer times, it is faster and it costs me pennies a month to run.

Leopold Kohr wrote it in 1957, long before the internet existed: "Wherever something is wrong, something is too big". Maybe we have spent years asking the wrong question. It doesn't matter so much whether a system is centralized, federated or distributed. What matters is whether it fits in the hands of someone you can write to when something breaks. Paul Ford, when he said goodbye to tilde.club, put it in writing: "you can, at any time, for very little money and relatively little effort, stand up a tiny digital community that basically belongs to itself".

So next time you are looking for a place to publish, to host your code or to talk with your friends, don't ask whether it is decentralized. Ask how many people are inside and whether you know the name of the person who runs it.

  • I had a couple drinks and woke up with 1,000 nerds, Paul Ford's account (2014) of how tilde.club was born and the flood of accounts in its first days.
  • Tildeverse, the association of tildes that followed the tilde.club model.
  • tilde.club, a shared Unix computer funded by its users' donations.
  • texto-plano.xyz, a Spanish-speaking tilde: "seamos pocos pero unidos" (let us be few but united).

item.title: [andros.dev] Org Social: the social network that survives its own infrastructure
item.description:
Org Social is so simple it looks like it was born before the internet. A single plain text file, an editor and a host are enough to interact with other people.

To "create an account", you just create a plain text file in any editor. Your "database" is your own hierarchy of posts. Your "algorithm" is however you decide to sort other people's posts. There is no "character limit". Your "server" is any hosting or web server. Your "interface" is your favorite editor. And if you want to "delete your account", you just delete the file. And of course, the syntax is richer than Markdown and just as easy to learn: Org Mode. You share and edit wherever you want, and you use it as a microblog, a journal, a forum, a bulletin board or a blog. Your file, your rules.

Behind it there is infrastructure that enriches the interaction and connects it with other systems and formats (the Fediverse, RSS, clients...). Each piece adds one more level of convenience, but none of them is essential: they are 100% optional! And that is what I want to talk about.

I'd like to take it apart piece by piece, explaining what each one does and why it exists.

Layer 0: a plain text file

Everything starts and ends here. A file called social.org, in UTF-8, with LF line endings.

The header is your profile. They are Org Mode keywords:

#+TITLE: My journal
#+NICK: Alice
#+DESCRIPTION: I write about Emacs and coffee
#+AVATAR: https://alice.com/avatar.jpg
#+LINK: https://alice.com
#+FOLLOW: https://bob.com/social.org
#+FOLLOW: friend https://carol.net/social.org

Below it, in a * Posts section, go your posts. Each one is a heading with an RFC 3339 timestamp, which works as a unique identifier:

** 2025-05-01T12:00:00+0100
:PROPERTIES:
:LANG: en
:TAGS: emacs org-social
:END:

Today I discovered Org Social and I can't stop writing.

And you already have a social network.

Anyone can curl your file, read it with their own eyes or with a client or script, and follow you by adding your URL to their #+FOLLOW:.

The interaction itself lives inside the format. There are no magic buttons, there are properties:

  • Replying is a post with :REPLY_TO: <url>#<id> pointing to the original.
  • Reacting is a reply with just :MOOD: ❤ and an empty body.
  • Sharing is :INCLUDE: with a reference to someone else's post.
  • Voting in a poll is replying with :POLL_OPTION:.
  • Mentioning someone is a link [[org-social:https://bob.com/social.org][Bob]].

Since it is plain text, you can edit all of it by hand if you feel like it.

When you are done, you save the file and upload it to your server.

Every decentralized social network has a weak spot, whichever one comes to mind. I covered this in There is no such thing as full decentralization, but in short, you always have to decide which of these five things the network sacrifices:

  • Identity
  • Connectivity
  • Discovery
  • Cost
  • Moderation

Org Social sacrifices discovery. Nobody can find you unless you give them your URL, just like an email address. And that makes some interactions impossible to reconstruct. For example, what happens if someone you don't follow joins a thread you started? If you don't follow them, you never find out.

That's why we need upper layers that mitigate the problem, although you should only use them if you think you need them. It may be that everyone taking part follows each other and needs nothing else. Otherwise, you will need a Relay: an index.

Layer 1: the client

You can check each feed directly with curl or with your browser. However, just like with your list of RSS/Atom feeds, what we all end up doing for convenience is using a client. It reads every source, sorts them, filters them and merges them into a list that is easier to read and that you can also navigate. The same goes for Org Social.

There is a client for Emacs, another for iOS, another for Android (in alpha as I write this), command line implementations and a public web viewer that needs no account or client. Clients build a timeline by merging all the feeds you follow, and they let you reply, react, share and vote in polls. But every change happens in your own file, not on a central server, and reading is volatile, since it is built on the fly.

The client also acts as a translator between Org Social and the interface you choose. And it is a good way in for people who are already used to X/Twitter or Mastodon, or who don't want to bother learning the syntax.

Layer 2: the Relay

The Relay is a server that crawls the network of social.org files and builds an index: users, mentions, replies, groups and threads. It does this by reading the #+FOLLOW: lines of every feed it knows and downloading the files it finds. You can also register your feed manually so it reads it.

It doesn't store content, only addresses. It notes who mentions whom, what replies to what and what belongs to each thread.

Now you can write a client or a script that asks the Relay for the information that fills in the parts where you were blind before:

# Who mentioned me?
curl "https://relay.org-social.org/notifications/?feed=..."

# Give me the full thread of this post
curl "https://relay.org-social.org/replies/?post=..."

# Find everything about Emacs
curl "https://relay.org-social.org/search/?q=emacs"

And that's not all: anyone can run their own Relay, locally or on a server. Their instance will connect to other public Relays and they will exchange information, so the whole network knows which feeds exist and how they relate.

It also offers other features, such as real-time notifications, RSS/Atom feeds, post search and bridges to ActivityPub/Mastodon. Yes, you can follow Mastodon accounts from Org Social, or keep up with Org Social from your favorite RSS/Atom reader.

Layer 3: Org Social Host

Needing your own hosting just to start taking part in the network is a tough requirement. That's why there is a free and open hosting service, integrated with the clients, that puts your social.org online with a single click.

You pick a nick and get two addresses:

  • public-url: the one you share with everyone, for example https://host.org-social.org/alice/social.org.
  • vfile: a secret, signed URL that works as a password. Whoever has it can overwrite your file, so keep it safe.

If you use a client, all of this is automatic and you never even see the secret URL, since it is stored in your configuration. It all happens behind the scenes.

If you are curious, signing up is a single request:

curl -X POST https://host.org-social.org/signup \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"nick": "alice"}'

And overwriting your file, another one:

curl -X POST https://host.org-social.org/upload \
  -F "vfile=YOUR_VFILE" \
  -F "file=@social.org"

It doesn't lock you in either. You can ask it for a permanent redirect (HTTP 301) to your new URL and your followers won't even notice. Their clients follow the redirect on their own, although it's a good idea to let them know so they update their #+FOLLOW:. It is a way in, not a requirement.

You can also run it on your own server, with public sign-up disabled and your own domain.

And it has an advantage that seasoned app developers will have guessed already: it makes syncing between devices easy. You can, for example, write in the mobile client and carry on in the Emacs one with simple HTTP requests. No old protocols, no third-party APIs.

Layer 4: Mirror or CDN

Do you use an RSS/Atom reader? Then you already know that the more feeds you follow, the slower it gets.

It doesn't matter how fast and parallel the downloads are. There will always be dropped connections, timeouts, errors and redirects. And if a feed is very large, the client has to parse all of it to keep what it cares about.

In my case, I follow 250 feeds. Download and parse them every time I scroll? Not viable. Cache them? Then the problem becomes when to invalidate the cache.

This is where the Mirror comes in. It is a server that keeps an up-to-date copy of every feed and saves you the parsing, sorting, thread building and mention consolidation. It exposes a simple REST API that returns JSON ready to use in a client.

You can think of it as a client of clients, or a general-purpose client without an interface. Internally, it works non-stop to keep the most recent copy and to prepare the processed information so it is easy to consume.

For example, if I want to build the timeline with Bob's and Carol's posts from the last 14 days:

curl --get "https://mirror.org-social.org/api/posts/" \
  --data-urlencode "following=https://bob.com/social.org" \
  --data-urlencode "following=https://carol.net/social.org" \
  --data-urlencode "sinceDays=14"

It doesn't replace the Relay. In fact, it needs it to know which feeds exist and which ones have changed. And most importantly: it is read-only. It never edits or deletes anything at the source. To publish, you still write to your own file. Its only way in is a webhook that a client can call to say a feed has changed and the Mirror should update it:

curl -X POST "https://mirror.org-social.org/api/webhook/refresh/" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"feed": "https://alice.com/social.org"}'

It is optional. The client calls it right after publishing or uploading a new version of the file to your hosting, so the Mirror updates its copy straight away instead of waiting for the next refresh cycle.

Layer 5: Push

The Relay already sends real-time notifications with Server-Sent Events, which clients can listen to in order to tell you about mentions, replies and reactions. But phones don't let an app keep connections open in the background, so there you need push notifications. It is the most specific layer of all, since each platform, iOS and Android, has its own notification system with its own certificates and tokens.

If this layer goes down, all you lose is the convenience of getting alerts on your phone while the app is closed.

Layer 6: Live Preview

An Org Social post has an address in the format https://<host>/social.org#<timestamp>. For example, my first post: https://host.org-social.org/andros/social.org#2025-08-14T09:11:00+0200. It works fine between Org Social clients, but what happens if you want to share it on another social network? Nothing pretty: the whole social.org file gets shared.

Live Preview turns a post into a web page. You give it the post URL, it downloads the original social.org (straight from the source, not through the Relay), finds the post and generates an HTML card with its Open Graph metadata: nick, avatar, text and date. Ready to share on any social network.

For example, the URL above becomes:

https://preview.org-social.org/?post=https%3A%2F%2Fhost.org-social.org%2Fandros%2Fsocial.org%232025-08-14T09%3A11%3A00%2B0200

And if I share it on social media, it looks like this:

Clients also use this link format in their share option.

The same need gave birth to another very interesting feature: generating an HTML blog from your social.org, if it is hosted on host.org-social.org.

For example, my Org Social web version would be preview.org-social.org/blog/andros.

You write in Org Mode, upload the file to the hosting (with a simple curl if you like) and your HTML blog is generated automatically, ready to share. It isn't perfect, since you don't control the design, but it saves you from running a static site generator.

Summary

In the end, they are not layers, but pieces orbiting around your social.org.

flowchart TB
    File["social.org"]
    Client["Client"]
    Relay["Relay"]
    Host["Host"]
    Mirror["Mirror"]
    Push["Push"]
    Preview["Live Preview"]

    Client -- "reads and writes" --> File
    Client -- "uploads and syncs" --> Host
    Host -- "hosts" --> File
    Host -- "registers feeds" --> Relay
    Relay -- "indexes" --> File
    Client -- "mentions, threads and search" --> Relay
    Mirror -- "which feeds exist and which change" --> Relay
    Mirror -- "copies" --> File
    Client -- "JSON timeline and webhook" --> Mirror
    Relay -- "real-time notifications" --> Push
    Push -- "phone alerts" --> Client
    Preview -- "reads" --> File
    Client -- "share link" --> Preview
Piece What it gives you If you remove it
social.org Your identity and your posts There is no network
Client Reading and writing comfortably You read with curl and edit by hand
Relay Discovery, mentions, threads and bridges You only see who you follow
Host Hosting without a server and syncing between devices You use your own hosting
Mirror Ready-to-use JSON, no Org parsing The client downloads and parses every file
Push Alerts on your phone You find out when you open the app
Live Preview Sharing posts outside the network You share the raw file URL

Whatever you use, the only essential piece is your social.org.

If every Org Social server shut down tomorrow, what would you lose? Convenience. And what would you keep? Your file, intact, on your disk. You upload it anywhere else and keep posting.

Few social networks can say the same.

item.title: [www.eferro.net] Turning up the dial: seeing the forest while working on any tree
item.description:
First post in a series about how I work at Clarity AI with an AI-native workspace. This one covers the experiment and the way of working; the next ones go deeper into specific pieces.

The forest problem

In April I decided to try to see the whole forest and still work on any tree, in any repo, owned by any team, without giving up on quality or on small, safe, sustainable steps. This post is how that went.

As Head of Engineering and Data Platform at Clarity AI, I have to look at the whole system all the time: dozens of repositories, many teams, data pipelines that depend on other data pipelines. If I only look at one repo, I miss what matters. If I only look at the whole, I lose contact with the code, and with it the ability to judge whether what we’re doing makes sense. The usual way out is a trade-off: you see the forest (meetings, documents, dashboards) and stop touching the trees, or you get into one tree and only hear about the rest secondhand. For years I lived somewhere in between, never comfortably.



The experiment: turning up the dial

Kent Beck described Extreme Programming as taking the practices that already work and turning the dial all the way up. If code reviews are good, review all the time. If testing is good, test all the time.

My experiment has two dials that move together. One is the practices I’ve trusted for years: small safe steps, TDD, trunk-based development, everything versioned, checking changes in the running system instead of stopping at the merge. The other is how much work I delegate to AI agents. What I’ve seen so far is that the second dial can only go as high as the first: delegating more without stronger practices just means breaking things faster. That’s an observation from one person over nearly six months, not something I’ve measured, and the rest of the post is the evidence I have for it, including where it falls short.



It started on 16 April 2026 as a git repository just for me, which I called platform-office, with a first commit called “bootstrap platform-office AI-native workspace”. The idea was modest: a place where an agent could find everything it needed, so I could stop re-explaining context in every session. The agents are Claude Code sessions, and the co-author trailers in the commits record which model made each change, and it changed over those months.

The mantra: everything is in the repo

One rule shaped everything else: if it’s not in the repo, it doesn’t exist.

That covers code, tasks, decisions, knowledge, communications with other teams, incidents, recaps, the skills the agents use, the tools those skills call, and even the engineering practices, packaged as skills. The company’s code repositories are not inside; they’re cloned when a task needs them. What I ended up with is a single repository for all the context around the code.

The first commit already had tasks/, decisions/, knowledge/ and five skills to manage them. Today it holds hundreds of tasks, decision records and knowledge documents, plus tracked communications, incidents and 45 skills, all plain Markdown with YAML front matter, readable by a person and parseable by an agent.


Writing all of that down is what lets an agent pick up any thread from a five-word prompt, and a colleague pick it up without asking me.

Keeping it that way meant going against the defaults. Agent harnesses like Claude Code (the program that runs the agent and enforces its permissions and hooks) save what the agent learns as personal memory, one user at a time. I wanted that knowledge to belong to the team and to anyone using the repo, so I had to be explicit: in August the agents were told to write what they learn into files in the repo, and a check blocks the commit if an instruction file points to private memory. On 10 September I moved the last personal memories worth keeping into the repo. A week later a colleague committed a piece of knowledge with the message “out of one laptop’s memory”.



How the work gets done: the skill families

A skill, as I use it here, is a flow with phases and gates (points where it stops and waits for a human decision), backed by deterministic tools in the same repo. There are 45, and they cluster into a few families: orienting the agent in the current state of the work, driving a task from capture to close, operations and incidents, the data platform, knowledge and decisions, cross-team communications, code quality, and setup and housekeeping. Several come from the practice skills I wrote about in Encoding Experience into AI Skills.

In practice, a session starts with a short sentence. Some kick off a flow: “run task X”, “look at this alert”, “let’s do a recap of what happened this week”. Others are open questions: “explain how system X works”, “let’s look at how we could improve the architecture of Y”. Either way, the agent loads the context it needs from the repo. It also looks up our organization inventory (more on it below) to find the code repositories related to the request, and clones them when it needs to read the code to give a better answer. Then it keeps working until it needs a decision from me.

Three of them are worth describing in more detail.

The task skill, po-do-task, runs a task through 14 phases and stops for a human decision only where it matters: before implementing, committing, pushing or talking to another team. The phases are: identify, take ownership, clarify, propose alternatives, implement with TDD, mutation testing, test desiderata, report, commit, push, watch CI, validate in the running system, close, and a mandatory postmortem, where the agent reviews what went wrong in the run and proposes changes to the skill itself. Those changes go back into the skill, which several people have rewritten many times.

The incident skill takes a single trigger (a Slack link, a failing pipeline, a pasted alert) through hypotheses and validation, works back from the immediate cause to the systemic one, and ends with follow-up tasks and a postmortem.

The summary skills look at a window of time instead of a single alarm. A census of the Kubernetes event stream complements alerting: it looks for steady signals that never cross a threshold, and proposes which ones deserve a closer look. A weekly health check runs five sources in parallel and crosses them. The manual sweep behind it found its best signal in that crossing: Airflow DAG issues clustering in the same afternoon window as memory pressure in a heavy batch process, which neither source showed on its own.

The principles, in practice

Looking back, the principles I wanted to follow show up in the commits.

See the forest

One repo holds the context of the whole platform, and the code repos a task needs are a command away. It didn’t start that way: I began with git submodules, and by late June there were dozens of them, copied again into every worktree, and the repo had become slow and heavy. On 12 July a decision record replaced them with plain clones on demand.

One code repository is the exception: our organization inventory, present in every session. It’s where Clarity keeps its governance data: dozens of teams and the repositories, Airflow DAGs, container images, Kubernetes deployments, S3 buckets, runtime applications and models each one owns, kept up to date automatically. The workspace reads it instead of copying it. So the first questions of any investigation are cheap: which repositories, applications and data pipelines relate to this topic, and which teams work on it. Even the catalogue of repos and the list of people who can own a task come from there.

Work on any tree

A task registered here is ours to finish, even when the fix lives in another team’s repository. The default is to diagnose the root cause, make the change and coordinate with the owners, with a tracked communication so they’re never surprised, rather than to open a ticket for them. The workspace brings the context; each repository keeps its own rules. A change in someone else’s repo follows that repo’s conventions, CI, review process and owners, in the same small steps as everything else.

Small, safe, sustainable steps

Two weeks in, the pre-commit hook was already running the whole test suite, and the workspace’s own tooling was being hardened with mutation testing. Everything goes trunk-based. Some things stay deliberately slow: any destructive change to live infrastructure is run by a person, one command at a time. The agent writes the exact command; a human runs it and reads the output.

Agents have no access of their own. They work with the access of whoever starts the session, and the rules every session loads keep the important steps in human hands: nothing is pushed, or sent to Slack or to another team, without an explicit go, and when someone approves a specific command, that exact command is what runs.

Experimentation and impact

From the first commit, every task declares its why and can be framed as a hypothesis. In May a validating state appeared: a merged change stays open until it’s checked in the running system. In August came discarded, because a well-argued “we’re not doing this” is also a result; 128 tasks have been discarded on purpose so far.

Learning

Corrections become rules or tools, and sometimes the right call is neither. In July I swept the agent sessions for repeated frictions and the conclusion was clear: rules that live only in documentation get violated; rules enforced by the harness, through hooks and checks, get followed. So corrections keep moving from text into checks, as the next section shows.

When the system got it wrong

Few of the failures I found were an agent doing something silly. Most were the system breaking in ways I hadn’t designed for, and more often than not it was the agent itself, in the mandatory postmortem, who noticed. Three patterns keep coming back.

Rules written as text get ignored; rules turned into tools get followed. A rule that said “use this fallback, the coverage plugin isn’t installed” was ignored in three separate tasks, with the rule in context every time. The postmortem concluded that a rule which has failed three times as prose becomes a make target. The same thing happened with links left behind when a task file moves: the skill first got a paragraph with a workaround, and then the task tool learned to repoint the links itself. When an instruction keeps failing, I stopped writing a better paragraph and changed the mechanism.

The system also has to check itself, including its own checks. One postmortem wrote its lessons into the wrong checkout and then said they were in the commit. Nothing contradicted it, because the working tree looked clean. Now it has to confirm that each lesson’s file shows up in the right git status. Mutation testing reported kill counts that were fake, because tests that crashed were counted as kills. A green pytest line turned out not to be the gate’s verdict. And when a postmortem proposed two more rules for a single friction, it rejected them, with the reason written down: a skill that grows on every friction stops being read.

Then there are the checks that weren’t what they looked like. A shortcut that was safe when someone wrote it stopped being safe once things around it changed. A check ran on every change and still stopped nothing, because nothing was wired to listen to it. A guard added to a shared tool was bypassed by skills that called the tool directly. In each case the check existed and was documented, but it relied on an assumption that was no longer true.

Each time a failure moved from a paragraph into a mechanism, I could delegate a bit more.

From a repo for me to a repo others use

In April, other people made 1% of the commits. In May it was 18%, and in August 46%, with ten people besides me contributing that month. Thirteen people have committed so far. Use keeps spreading, slowly, to other teams and individuals, although most of the commits still come from a few of us.



What surprised me is that nobody came to “use Eduardo’s tools”. They came with their own problem: running our data pipelines, Snowflake operations, migrating services between platforms, alert noise per squad. The repo gave them context and a mechanism, and several of them then started improving the system: seven of the 45 skills were written by someone else, and one colleague launched an initiative to make the workspace’s context cheaper for every session.

None of them adopted the whole thing, and none of them had to. You don’t need to file tasks, record decisions or run the 14-phase flow to get value from the repo. The pieces are useful on their own and they compose: you can start by reading the knowledge base, pick up one skill weeks later, and register a task or a communication only when it helps. I suspect that’s a big part of why adoption happened without a mandate.

For people who are new to the repo, those open questions are usually the way in. With the context of the whole platform in one place, anyone can open a session and say “this is my situation, I want to do this, how is it done at Clarity?”, and get an answer grounded in our decisions, runbooks and code. A colleague who started using it recently told me it had given him more onboarding than any person had. That kind of use leaves almost no trace in git, so the charts undercount it.

The first time the tooling broke because I wasn’t its only user came in June, when two of us created different decision records with the same number, three times in a week. Sequential IDs assume a single author. Random suffixes on every ID fixed it: a small change, but one you only make when the tool has to work for more than one person.

Then I stepped away. Between 20 August and 1 September I made zero commits, and the repo got 191 commits from six other people.


On 6 September we recorded what was already true: the workspace is open to anyone at Clarity, and nobody has to go through me to use it or change it. I steward it: I maintain the tooling, review what lands on main and run the nightly loops. The deeper changes of direction still tend to come from me, mostly because that’s the easy path, not because anyone has to ask.

What I haven’t solved yet

Two problems grow at the same pace as adoption, and I don’t have good answers for either yet.

Integration with the company’s task system

The repo is the source of truth for our work, but the company runs on Jira, and keeping the two in sync is manual: a task here, its mirror ticket there, keys copied by hand. Many commits cite a Jira key in the subject line alone, and some exist only to say “mirror ticket created” or “comment posted”. One housekeeping skill exists only to stop GitLab from turning our DR-NNN and INC-NNN references into links to Jira tickets that don’t exist. I haven’t decided which direction the sync should go, or how to avoid double bookkeeping without breaking “everything is in the repo”. I’m running a few experiments on exactly that right now.

Pruning, cleaning and compacting the knowledge base

“Everything in the repo” also means everything accumulates. Since April, 602 knowledge documents have been added and 30 deleted, with a single explicit cleanup in July. The instruction file every agent session loads grew from about 430 words to about 4,600. Disk space is the least of it: every session spends part of its context on what nobody has pruned, and outdated knowledge is worse than missing knowledge, because an agent treats it as true. My idea is a weekly routine, like the health check, that detects duplicates, stale documents and contradictions with the code or with newer decisions, and proposes the compaction as a reviewable change. The agent proposes, a human decides. It’s not automated yet.

What I’m not claiming

Commits are activity, not value, and many are the workspace’s own bookkeeping. This is not a controlled experiment: one person driving it, better models arriving during the same months, people who were already hands-on. I haven’t compared the workflow against a small guide alone, so I can’t tell how much of the result is the system and how much is the model doing well by itself. The 191 commits from six people in the 13 days I made none tell me the repo works without me. They don’t tell me people would use it if I weren’t the one asking. Writing everything down has a real cost I feel but haven’t measured. And none of this is autonomous: a human approves every push and runs every destructive change, on purpose.

What I can say is how it feels from the inside. The feedback from the people using it has been very good, and I’ve never been this productive, above all on cross-cutting problems, the ones that touch many teams and repos at once and usually stall. That’s an impression, not a measurement, but it’s a strong one.

What comes next

In the next posts I’ll take apart some of the skill families and some of the subsystems behind them, like communications and task management. I’ll pick the order as I go.

And if you lead a platform or engineering team: which of these problems are you fighting right now?
